19560.title: Add unique tie-breaker to default cursor pagination ordering
19560.body:
Cursor pagination derives its cursor from the sorting fields in use. When a connection falls back to the model's `Meta.ordering` and that ordering is not unique, the cursor cannot identify a single row, so the "everything after this cursor" filter is wrong for any group of rows sharing the same values:

- if the trailing ordering value is NULL, `_prepare_filter` skips the field entirely and the resulting filter matches the whole queryset, so the same page is served over and over and `endCursor` never advances;
- otherwise the filter jumps past the entire group, silently dropping every remaining row in it.

`productVariants` hits both cases. `ProductVariant.Meta.ordering` is `("sort_order", "sku")`: `sort_order` is scoped per product, so it repeats across the global connection and is NULL for bulk created variants, and `sku` is optional. `Webhook.eventDeliveries` and `EventDelivery.attempts` hit the second case, as both order by `created_at` alone and deliveries fanned out for a single event are bulk created on the same timestamp.

Fix it once in `sort_queryset_by_default`, which every default-ordered connection routes through, by appending `pk` to the ordering when it does not already contain a primary key. `pk` is unique and never NULL, so every cursor now identifies exactly one row. Appending it does not reorder distinct keys, it only makes ties deterministic.

Note that cursors gain a component, so cursors issued before this change are rejected with "Received curs

19678.body:
`MAX_IMAGE_FILE_SIZE` bounds the *encoded* size of an image, which says nothing about the memory needed to decode it. An 8000×8000 WebP is 0.11 MB on disk but needs ~1 GB of RAM to decode. Pillow's built-in guard doesn't help at defaults: it warns above ~89M pixels and only raises above twice that, so a 64M-pixel image passes silently.

This PR adds a `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` setting (default 30M ≈ 5000×5000, configurable via env var) enforced through `Image.MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS`, so it covers every place we decode an image. The check runs while parsing the image header, so an oversized image is rejected before any pixel memory is allocated.

## Before

- An image was only validated by encoded file size (10 MB), so a tiny highly-compressed file with a huge pixel count passed validation.
- Decoding such an image (e.g. thumbnail generation) could exhaust the worker's memory.
- Pillow's `DecompressionBombWarning`/`Error` fired only at ~89M/178M pixels, with no reference to which object was being processed.

- Any decode of an image above `MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS` raises immediately at header-parse time, without allocating decode memory.
- **Uploads** (product/collection/user media): rejected with the existing `FILE_SIZE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` error code — no GraphQL schema change.
- **Thumbnail view**: returns `400 Image is too large.` for a stored oversized image.
- **`fetch_product_media_image_task`**: treats it as an expected, non-retryable failure (new `ImageTooLargeErr

19766.body:
## Why this matters

A merchant reported an order stuck showing **Overcharged** even though the customer paid exactly the order total. Everything in the API agreed with itself — `total.gross == totalCharged`, `grantedRefunds: []`, `totalBalance: 0`, a single transaction with a single `pspReference` — and yet the stored `chargeStatus` said `OVERCHARGED`.

19794.title: Fix `giftCardBulkCreate` removing existing tags from previously created gift cards
19794.body:
I want to merge this change because `giftCardBulkCreate` silently removes a tag from every gift card that already carried it whenever the request reuses that tag.

Will be ported to `3.23` and main.

Fixes #19768

`GiftCardBulkCreate.assign_gift_card_tags` attached the new cards with `tag_instance.gift_cards.set(instances)`. Django's `set()` replaces the whole relation, so for an already existing tag every previously tagged card lost it. The fix is forward-only. Tag links already lost cannot be recovered from the database. Merchants can restore the tagging of older batches from their own records, for example by re-tagging with `giftCardUpdate` and `addTags`.

19878.title: Filter products by externalReference
19878.body:
Adds an `externalReference` filter to `ProductWhereInput`, so integrations can fetch many products by their external IDs in a single request:

```graphql
products(where: { externalReference: { oneOf: ["ext-1", "ext-2", "ext-3"] } }) { ... }
```

I want to merge this change because syncing integrations currently have to issue one `product(externalReference: ...)` query per product. With `oneOf` they can resolve a whole batch at once.

## Changes

- Filter: `ProductWhere.external_reference` (`StringFilterInput`, `eq` / `oneOf`) using the same `filter_where_by_value_field` helper as `slug` and `name`. `Product.external_reference` is already unique and indexed, so no migration is needed.
- Because `ProductWhereInput` is shared, the filter is also available in `Category.products(where:)`, `Collection.products(where:)` and promotion catalogue `productPredicate`.
- The legacy `filter: ProductFilterInput` is not extended; no legacy filter input has an external reference filter.
- API documentation: updates the generated GraphQL schema, adds an `ADDED_IN_323` label, and includes a changelog entry.

## Behavior notes

Edge cases follow the shared helper, consistent with `slug`/`name`:
- `{eq: ""}`, `{oneOf: []}`, `{oneOf: null}`, `{}` and `null` return no products.
- `{eq: null}` returns products **without** an external reference.

- 182 tests in `test_products_query_with_where.py` and `test_collection_query.py` pass. New coverage: `eq` match/no match/empty/null, `oneOf`

19963.title: Fix OIDC last_login duplicate writes and refresh check ignoring days
19963.body:
I want to merge this change because it fixes two bugs in how OIDC logins update `last_login`. Follow-up to #19960, it's part of the same initiative aiming to reduce number of database writes

**Duplicate writes on parallel requests.** Requests authenticated with an OIDC JWT access token set `last_login` to the token's issue time when it's newer than the stored value. The check runs on a copy of the user read from the replica, and the save was unconditional. When a client sends several requests at once with a new token, for example a mobile app opening, every request saw the old value, wrote `last_login` to the same `account_user` row and triggered a `CUSTOMER_UPDATED` webhook. While the replica lags, more requests fall into that window. A request with an older token could also move `last_login` backwards.

The write is now a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE last_login IS NULL OR last_login < <issue time>`, so only the request that moves `last_login` forward writes the row and triggers the webhook.

**Refresh check ignoring whole days.** The OIDC login flow and opaque access tokens refresh `last_login` only when it's older than `OAUTH_UPDATE_LAST_LOGIN_THRESHOLD` (15 minutes by default). The check used `timedelta.seconds`, which drops whole days, so a user who last logged in 1 day and 10 minutes ago looked like they logged in 10 minutes ago, and `last_login` wasn't updated. It now uses `total_seconds()`.
